title: Jacob Blesses Pharaoh; Joseph and the Famine
summary: Joseph presents five of his brothers and then his father to Pharaoh, who grants them the best of the land in Goshen, and the aged Jacob blesses the king. As the famine deepens, Joseph sells grain to the Egyptians first for money, then for livestock, and finally for their land and their labor, so that the land becomes Pharaoh's and the people pay him a fifth of their harvest. Israel prospers in Goshen, and near death Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him with his fathers in Canaan.
story: Jacob's family has arrived, and this chapter settles them. Two scenes before Pharaoh secure their place in Goshen, and then the narrative steps back to show what the famine did to Egypt as a whole under Joseph's administration. The contrast is deliberate: while the Egyptians lose their money, their herds, and finally their land, the Israelites acquire property and are fruitful and multiply (v. 27), the language of God's blessing on creation (1:28) and on Jacob (35:11). The chapter closes with Jacob near death, looking past Egypt to the promised land. Genesis is moving toward its last scenes, the blessing of Joseph's sons (Genesis 48), Jacob's words over all twelve sons (Genesis 49), and the burial and death that end the book (Genesis 50).
historical:
Pharaoh settles the family in the district of Rameses (v. 11), another name for Goshen. The city of Rameses was built by Ramesses II in the thirteenth century BC, so the name is probably a later updating of the place name for readers who knew the region by that name, much as Genesis 14:14 calls a city Dan long before it had that name. Some scholars take such names instead as signs of a late date of composition.

In Egyptian ideology the king owned the land in principle, but in practice land was held by temples, officials, and families, and temples controlled vast estates. Royal decrees survive that exempt temples and their staff from state levies and forced labor, which fits the note that the priests kept their land and received rations from Pharaoh (v. 22). Joseph's policy concentrates the land in the crown in exchange for survival, fixing a permanent tax of a fifth of the harvest. The narrator's comment that this remained in force “to this day” (v. 26) speaks from a later vantage point, explaining an arrangement Israelite readers knew.
cultural:
Jacob gives his age as 130 and calls his years few and hard compared with those of his fathers; Abraham lived to 175 and Isaac to 180 (25:7; 35:28). The word he uses for his life, sojourning, describes the status of a resident foreigner without land of his own, which is exactly how the patriarchs lived in Canaan (see the word note). That this landless old man blesses the king of Egypt, twice (vv. 7, 10), would have struck an ancient reader, since blessing normally flows from the greater to the lesser.

The oath at the end of the chapter follows an old form. Putting the hand under the thigh, as Abraham's servant did in 24:2, was a solemn gesture associated with the source of a man's descendants, binding the one who swore to the family's future. Jacob asks Joseph for kindness and faithfulness (the Hebrew chesed and emet), the loyalty owed within a covenant relationship. Burial with one's ancestors mattered deeply; for Jacob it also meant burial in the land God had promised, at the cave of Machpelah where Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, and Leah lay (49:29-32).
literary: The chapter falls into four scenes. The brothers before Pharaoh (vv. 1-6) and Jacob before Pharaoh (vv. 7-12) carry out Joseph's plan from 46:31-34. The famine policy (vv. 13-26) is told as a sequence of three exchanges, each triggered by the people's plea: money for grain, livestock for grain, and finally land and bodies for seed. The pace is steady and the narrator offers no judgment. The final scene (vv. 27-31) returns to Israel. The ironies are carefully placed. The Egyptians sell themselves as slaves to Pharaoh; in Exodus the Israelites will be made slaves by a later Pharaoh. The Egyptians lose their land while the Israelites gain it. And the chapter ends with Israel bowing in worship at the head of his bed, a patriarch in Egypt whose heart is set on Canaan.

outline.t: Jacob blesses Pharaoh and the family settles in Goshen
The famine and Joseph's land policy
Israel prospers, and Jacob asks to be buried in Canaan

doctrines.note: God promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (12:3). Here Abraham's grandson, a foreigner dependent on Egypt's bread, blesses the most powerful king of his world. Israel's calling to bring blessing to the nations is visible even when it has nothing to offer but a blessing.

Jacob will die in Egypt, but he refuses to be buried there. His request, “carry me out of Egypt and bury me with them”, is an act of hope in God's promise of the land, and it anticipates the exodus of his descendants.

Hebrews 11:21 lists Jacob's final act of worship among the deeds of faith. Faith here is not success; Jacob calls his life few and hard. It is the settled conviction, at the end of a troubled life, that God's promise is more real than Egypt's plenty.

words.note: Magur, sojourning, the life of a resident alien. Jacob calls his whole life, and his fathers' lives, years of sojourning (v. 9; the BSB renders it travels). The patriarchs lived in the promised land without owning it, apart from a burial cave. The New Testament picks up this theme when it calls the patriarchs strangers and exiles on the earth, seeking a homeland (Hebrews 11:13-14).

Barak, to bless. Jacob blesses Pharaoh on arriving and again on leaving (vv. 7, 10). Some translators take the first as a respectful greeting, but in Genesis blessing is more than courtesy; it is a word that carries God's favor. The verb ties this scene to the promise of blessing that runs through Genesis from 1:28 and 12:2-3.

Mittah, bed or couch. Israel bowed in worship at the head of his bed (v. 31). The Hebrew consonants of this word are the same as those for staff (matteh), and the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation) read staff here. Hebrews 11:21 follows that reading, saying Jacob worshiped leaning on the top of his staff. Both readings picture an old man worshiping at the end of his strength.

christ: The chapter's links to Christ are thematic. Abraham's family was chosen to bring blessing to the nations, and here Jacob blesses Pharaoh; Paul says that Scripture foresaw God justifying the Gentiles by faith and announced the gospel beforehand to Abraham in the promise that all nations would be blessed through him (Galatians 3:8), a promise he sees fulfilled in Christ. The starving Egyptians' words to Joseph, “You have saved our lives”, belong to the Joseph story's picture of one man through whom a whole world is fed, a theme Christians have heard again in Jesus' claim to be the bread of life (John 6:35). And Jacob's description of his life as sojourning becomes, in Hebrews 11, the posture of all God's people, who live as strangers looking for the city God has prepared, a hope the letter grounds in Christ.

hard.q: Did Joseph enslave the Egyptians? How should we judge his famine policy?
hard.a:
The chapter reports that Joseph acquired all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh and that the people became Pharaoh's servants in exchange for food, paying a fifth of their harvest thereafter. There is also a textual question in verse 21. The traditional Hebrew text says Joseph moved the people to the cities, while the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint say he made them slaves, a reading the BSB follows.

Readers judge the policy differently. Some see it as wise crisis administration. The people themselves offered their land and labor, they thank Joseph for saving their lives, the tax of a fifth left them four-fifths of the harvest, and without the stored grain they would have died. Others read the chapter more critically, noting that Joseph concentrated wealth and power in Pharaoh's hands in a way Israel's own law would later forbid; the law of Leviticus 25 says the land cannot be sold permanently and that Israelites must not be made permanent slaves. They also note the irony that the centralized power Joseph built becomes the machine that later enslaves his own people. The narrator offers no explicit verdict, and a careful reading can honor Joseph's life-saving work while recognizing that Scripture does not present every policy of a faithful man as a model.

questions: Jacob calls his 130 years few and hard, yet he blesses the most powerful man in the world. What does it look like to bless others out of a life that has been difficult?
The Egyptians traded everything to survive. In what ways do people today trade their freedom for security, and when is that trade wise or unwise?
Jacob lived in Egypt's plenty but asked to be buried in the land of promise. Where is your heart's true home, and how does that show in the way you plan for the end of your life?
